title: Son of Gautami, Son of Vasishthi

title_i18n.en: Son of Gautami, Son of Vasishthi

subtitle: Mothers, Names and Power in the Satavahana Deccan
era: Matronymic titulature across the dynasty, c. 1st-3rd century CE
region: Nashik, Karla, Kanheri and the wider Deccan
moral: Names can carry alliances as well as ancestry.

sources.citation: Nashik, Karla and Kanheri donor inscriptions, especially Epigraphia Indica Vol. 8
sources.note: Epigraphic evidence for matronymic royal names and women donors.

sources.citation: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India (2008)
sources.note: Clear modern explanation that matronymics do not prove matriarchy.

sources.citation: Richard Salomon, Indian Epigraphy (1998); Andrew Ollett, Language of the Snakes (2017)
sources.note: Epigraphic and language context for women's public inscriptions.

panels.shot: low-angle wide of rock-cut cave façade with queenly figure in foreground

dialogue.text: In the basalt cliffs of the Deccan, kings name themselves after mothers: Gautamiputra, Vasishthiputra. What power did these women wield, that stone must remember them?

panels.shot: slow push-in on a bird’s-eye view of the Western Ghats and Godavari valley

dialogue.text: The Deccan in the first centuries of our era is a land of roads and rivers, caravans and caves, where the Satavahana kings hold the plateaus between north and south.

panels.shot: medium close-up on a hand carving letters into rock

dialogue.text: Their history does not survive in court chronicles. It lives in chiselled lines at Nashik, Karla and Kanheri, where donors speak in stone.

panels.shot: close-up profile of Satavahana Royal Patroness reading an inscription

dialogue.text: There we first glimpse the royal women: queens, mothers, nuns, merchant wives. Not in gossip, but in their own words, recorded as donors.

panels.shot: medium shot inside a Nashik cave with monks in background

dialogue.text: One inscription at Nashik names a royal mother donating a cave and cistern to monks. Her gift is a place to sit, sleep and endure the Deccan heat and rain.

panels.shot: low-angle medium of patroness with stylised kingly figure in background silhouette

dialogue.text: Yet when her son speaks in stone, he does something unusual for ancient India: he names himself not only as someone’s son, but as the son of his mother.

panels.shot: extreme close-up of letters forming ‘Gautamiputrasa’ on rock

dialogue.text: ‘Gautamiputrasa’ says a line, ‘the son of Gautami’. Elsewhere another king is ‘Vasishthiputrasa’, the son of Vasishthi. The pattern repeats, again and again.

panels.shot: slow push-in on patroness seated in a council hall with men around

dialogue.text: To some modern eyes this looks like a matriarchal court, where mothers rule and trace descent. But the stone is quieter than that. It tells us something smaller, and more precise.

panels.shot: split-panel style composition showing two queens with different families behind them

dialogue.text: Satavahana kings married more than once. Each mother brought her own lineage: brahmana clans, regional chiefs, merchant houses. A prince’s mother meant a prince’s allies.

panels.shot: medium shot of patroness placing a hand on a young prince’s shoulder before elders

dialogue.text: In such a house, a name is a promise. When a king calls himself ‘Gautamiputra’, he publicly ties his throne to his mother’s people. It is alliance, carved as identity.

panels.shot: low-angle wide of patroness supervising artisans at Karla cave entrance

dialogue.text: And the same women move beyond the palace. At Karla and Kanheri, inscriptions show queens and merchant wives donating halls, pillars, cisterns, even entire villages to monastic communities.

panels.shot: close-up of patroness handing a small clay seal or token to a monk

dialogue.text: The language of these records is clear. The property is hers to give. Land and revenue flow from her name into religious networks, and the law—whatever its exact form—recognizes her capacity.

panels.shot: medium shot of a woman merchant and a nun standing together in a cave verandah

dialogue.text: Nor are royal women alone. In the same scripts, nuns and merchant wives appear as donors. The world of names and gifts is not confined to the palace.

panels.shot: extreme close-up on patroness’s thoughtful eyes as torchlight flickers

dialogue.speaker: satavahana_royal_women
dialogue.text: If his name carries me, my kin must never doubt his throne.

panels.shot: diagrammatic-style wide of inscriptions in different scripts and regions

dialogue.text: Scholars reading these scattered stones see a pattern. Matronymic names cluster within the Satavahana house, not across all society. They signal marriage politics, not a wholesale matrilineal order.

panels.shot: medium shot of a modern scholar in a library examining estampages

dialogue.text: Without a surviving Satavahana law code, the rest is careful inference. Epigraphy, language and comparison help reconstruct the legal space in which these women acted.

panels.shot: wide shot of patroness walking away from a completed cave at dusk

dialogue.text: When the last chisel falls silent, the cave remains. Generations forget her face, but not her name. It survives as a matronymic, wrapped around her son’s royal claims.

panels.shot: slow pull-back from patroness’s name carved beside a king’s name

dialogue.text: This is the quiet revolution of the Satavahana women: not overthrowing men, but inscribing themselves into the very names of kings, so that every royal title must also whisper a mother’s lineage.
